values.value: MCP Is the USB-C of AI
One standard plug instead of a drawer full of adapters: why the Model Context Protocol makes connecting AI to your tools boring in the best possible way.

value.markup:
Remember the drawer? The one full of chargers, each with a slightly different plug, each fitting exactly one device you no longer own. For years, connecting an AI model to your own tools felt just like that drawer. Every assistant needed its own bespoke integration, every API needed its own glue code, and every new model meant starting over.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the moment the industry agreed on a single plug. A tool author writes one MCP server, and any MCP-capable client (a chat app, an IDE, a coding agent) can use it straight away. That's the whole trick, and it turns out to be a very big trick.

values.value: One kind of cable, endless devices. Photo: Lucian Alexe on Unsplash

value.markup:
Write once, plug in everywhere

Before MCP, connecting M models to N tools meant building M × N integrations. With a shared protocol it becomes M + N: each tool exposes one server, each client speaks one protocol, and they meet in the middle. Tool authors get reach, client authors get an ecosystem, and users get to pick both freely.

MCP servers describe their own capabilities: tools with typed inputs, resources to read, prompts to reuse. A client doesn't need to be taught what a CMS, a database or a ticketing system can do; it asks the server, and the server tells it in a format every client understands.

values.value: A protocol is a promise: if you speak this, I'll understand you.

value.markup:
Boring, in the best way

The highest compliment you can pay a standard is that people stop talking about it. Nobody gets excited about plugging in a USB-C cable; it just works. MCP is heading the same way: once your tools speak it, connecting a new assistant is a configuration line, not a project.

That frees everyone to focus on the interesting part: what the assistant actually does with the access it now has. Which is exactly where the fun starts.

values.value: Why MCP Makes Your CMS Talk Back
This very site was modelled, filled and published by an AI assistant talking to Umbraco over MCP. Here's what that feels like, and why it matters.

value.markup:
Here's a confession: nobody clicked through the Umbraco backoffice to build this blog. The document types, the block grid, the media library and the very words you're reading were all created by an AI assistant calling Umbraco's MCP servers, one well-described tool at a time.

That's not a party trick. It's a glimpse of how content management changes when your CMS can explain itself to an assistant: what types exist, what a property expects, which pages are live. The assistant stops guessing and starts asking the system directly.

values.value: The best integration is the one you never had to write.
Every developer who has maintained a bespoke API connector

value.markup:
Two servers, two jobs

This project runs two MCP servers side by side. One is for developers: it creates data types, document types, templates and media. The other is for editors: it creates pages, adds blocks and publishes. Splitting them means each assistant only sees the tools that fit its role, and an editor's assistant can't accidentally redesign the schema.

  • Self-describing: a tool can hand back the exact JSON shape a media picker expects, so nothing is guessed.
  • Safe by default: drafts stay drafts until something explicitly publishes them.
  • Verifiable: every write can be read straight back to confirm it landed.

values.value: Many parts, one structure. Photo: Alina Grubnyak on Unsplash

value.markup:
Conventions still win

Giving an assistant access is only half the story. This project has firm conventions: where document types live, how blocks render, how files are named. MCP doesn't replace them. Instead the assistant follows them, because the tools make the right way the easy way.

The result is a CMS you can talk to without it turning into a mess. Ask for a blog, get a blog, and still recognise the codebase the next morning. That, more than any demo, is why MCP is awesome.
